result: The authors established multipatch setups with 10 Sensapex and 8 Scientifica manipulators using custom-made stages with optimized geometry (27° approach angle, aluminum/steel construction) and integrated hardware for simultaneous 10-channel recording.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 describe the physical setup with specific technical details (manipulator types, stage materials, approach angles, amplifier configuration) that are documented in methods and shown in Figure 1. The technical specifications are concrete and verifiable.

result: An automated pressure control system was developed that can be built within one week with basic equipment, uses multiple pressure levels (20 mbar LOW, 70 mbar HIGH), and is applicable to any patch-clamp setup to reduce errors and increase experimental speed.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 and C72-C76 describe the pressure system with specific technical parameters and benefits. The system is documented in Figure 2 with detailed schematics. While the claimed benefits (C76) are somewhat speculative, the core technical achievement is well-documented.

result: Pipette cleaning using Alconox solution enables immediate reuse with >10 successful repatches. In rat pyramidal neurons (n=67), no systematic changes in cellular or synaptic properties were detected after cleaning (p>0.05, mean relative differences 0-10%), validating the cleaning protocol.
evaluation: Claims C36-C38 present quantitative validation data from 67 rat neurons with appropriate statistical testing (repeated measures ANOVA, p>0.05) shown in Figure 3I-L. The validation is thorough, though the authors appropriately note limitations and recommend user-specific validation (methods text).

result: Performance benchmarking across 6-, 8-, and 10-pipette configurations showed declining success rates (88±12%, 85±13%, 79±11%) and increasing experimental times (36.6±2.3 min to 46.1±4.6 min) as pipette numbers increased, with tested connections scaling from 23±7 to 56±17.
evaluation: Claims C39-C43 present systematic performance data with sample sizes (n=30, 33, 10) and quantitative metrics shown in Figure 4B-D. The declining success rate with increased pipette numbers is well-documented and supports the conclusion (C88) that conventional scaling becomes impractical.

result: The clean-to-complete strategy increased average cluster sizes to 7.8±0.4 (97±5% success rate, n=16) for 8 pipettes and 9.2±0.6 (92±6% success rate, n=9) for 10 pipettes by enabling immediate cleaning and reuse of failed pipettes during experiments.
evaluation: Claim C44 presents quantitative improvements with sample sizes shown in Figure 5B-C. The success rates represent substantial improvements over conventional approaches (C39-C42), demonstrating the practical benefit of the cleaning system.

result: The clean-to-extend strategy increased tested connections from 140±24 to 244±52 per animal (n=6) on the 8-pipette setup. Distance distributions remained similar across recording rounds (median 84-85 μm), indicating no systematic spatial bias.
evaluation: Claim C45 presents quantitative data with sample size shown in Figure 5D-E. Claim C94 addresses potential spatial bias with distance analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), strengthening the conclusion that sequential patching doesn't introduce systematic artifacts.

result: Using two rounds of clean-to-extend, up to 17 neighboring neurons were recorded in one human slice, with two neurons maintained across all sessions to probe complex connectivity patterns including their connections to 16 other neurons.
evaluation: Claims C46-C98 describe a specific experimental demonstration shown in Figure 6A-D. The connectivity matrix clearly shows the 17 neurons and detected connections, providing direct visual evidence for the claimed capability.

result: Using two setups simultaneously, 300-700 potential synaptic connections were probed from individual human patients within 24 hours (up to 99 neurons recorded), generating sample sizes comparable to previous studies that pooled multiple subjects.
evaluation: Claims C47 and C22 present the throughput achievement shown in Figure 6E-F with data from three patients (336-694 tested connections). Claim C99 contextualizes this with citations to previous pooled studies, demonstrating the advance in per-patient data yield.

result: Excitatory connectivity between pyramidal cells in human cortical layer 2/3 ranged from 12.9-17.7% across three patients, similar to previous reports. Inter-individual differences were not statistically different (p>0.05) but were statistically equivalent within ±5-9.5%.
evaluation: Claims C48-C49 present connectivity measurements with appropriate statistical testing (Fisher's exact test, equivalence testing with 90% CI) shown in Figure 6G. The comparison to previous studies (C100) with citations validates the measurements and demonstrates consistency.

result: Optimizations including a prefill device and semi-automated pipette positioning reduced preparation times to 11-13 minutes for filling/mounting and 7-9 minutes for positioning, as shown in Figure 4C.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 present specific time measurements shown in Figure 4C. These are straightforward timing measurements that support the efficiency improvements, though they represent incremental optimizations rather than major innovations.

result: The semi-automated approach achieved higher success rates (88%/85%/79%) than fully automated systems (43-51%) and faster positioning (53-55 s/pipette vs 103 s), though manual patching took slightly longer (126-154 s vs 120 s), leading to the conclusion that full automation would require disproportionate effort.
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 compare performance to published automated systems with specific citations (Wu et al., 2016; Kolb et al., 2019). The comparison is quantitative and supports the authors' assessment (C128) that their hybrid approach represents a practical optimum, though this conclusion involves some subjective judgment.

result: The combined improvements represent a substantial increase in experimental output compared to previous studies requiring data pooling across subjects, enabling microcircuit analysis at the individual patient level and potentially reducing animal numbers needed for statistically significant findings.
evaluation: Claims C101-C103 and C143 synthesize the overall impact with appropriate citations (Seeman et al., 2018; Thomson and Lamy, 2007). The conclusion is well-supported by the demonstrated throughput (C47, C99) and validated measurements (C48-C49), representing the main contribution of the work.

result: The authors discuss that underestimation of synaptic connectivity in slice experiments is an ongoing concern, with correction factors ranging from 1.1-1.7 depending on the source of error (axon cutting vs detection limits), and recommend avoiding superficial cells and controlling for distance and recording quality.
evaluation: Claims C113-C119 present a balanced discussion of methodological limitations with appropriate citations to the relevant literature. This represents a thoughtful consideration of potential systematic errors rather than a novel finding, appropriately placed in the discussion.

result: The authors compare multipatch to alternative methods (all-optical approaches, calcium/voltage imaging, optogenetic stimulation), noting that while these can probe more neurons (20-200), multipatch provides superior access to cellular/synaptic properties, doesn't require genetic modification, and is uniquely suited for measuring synaptic strength and plasticity.
evaluation: Claims C132-C142 provide a comprehensive comparison to alternative methods with appropriate citations throughout. This represents a fair assessment of the trade-offs between methods, appropriately acknowledging both advantages and limitations of the multipatch approach.
